events.title: Memcached released
events.summary: Brad Fitzpatrick added Memcached to LiveJournal on May 22, 2003 — a distributed in-memory cache that offloads hot reads from databases.
events.about: Memcached stores key-value blobs in RAM across a pool of servers — Facebook, Wikipedia, and early web giants used it to survive traffic spikes. Teams cache SQL query results, session data, and HTML fragments with `get`/`set` and TTL expiry. Redis later added richer data types; Memcached stayed the simple, fast cache layer.

narrative.whyChosen: Memcached pioneered the 'cache in front of the database' pattern for high-traffic web apps.
narrative.whyImportant: It made horizontal scaling of read-heavy sites practical before cloud managed caches existed.
narrative.problemSolved: Repeating expensive database queries on every page view could not scale LiveJournal and similar sites.

events.title: WordPress released
events.summary: Matt Mullenweg and Mike Little released WordPress 0.7 on May 27, 2003 — a fork of b2/cafelog that became the world's most-used CMS.
events.about: WordPress powers blogs, marketing sites, WooCommerce stores, and headless CMS backends — themes, plugins, and a familiar admin UI on any PHP host. It democratized publishing for non-developers while staying hackable for agencies. Today it runs a large share of the public web.

narrative.whyChosen: WordPress became the default way to publish on the web without building a CMS from scratch.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved open-source PHP could dominate consumer publishing and plugin ecosystems at global scale.
narrative.problemSolved: Blogging tools like b2 were stagnating; developers needed a maintained, extensible fork with a modern admin.

events.title: CSS Zen Garden launched
events.summary: Dave Shea launched the CSS Zen Garden in May 2003 — a collaborative gallery where designers restyle one HTML page using only CSS.
events.about: The Zen Garden answered skeptics who still treated CSS as a novelty: hundreds of designers submitted radically different skins of the same markup, proving presentation could be fully separated from structure. It became a teaching reference and helped convince agencies to abandon table-based layouts.

narrative.whyChosen: The Zen Garden showed what CSS could do better than any specification document.
narrative.whyImportant: It accelerated the shift from table layouts and font tags to standards-based design.
narrative.problemSolved: Many teams still doubted CSS could match the visual richness of table hacks and spacer GIFs.
